questions.question: Explain how differential erosion in horizontally layered rocks produces the Karoo's landform family, naming each landform in its erosional sequence.
questions.expected_answer: The Karoo Supergroup consists of horizontally layered shales, mudstones and sandstones intruded by resistant dolerite sills. Because the layers differ in strength, weathering and erosion strip the soft layers quickly while the hard layers survive — differential erosion. A resistant cap rock shields the soft layers beneath it, so protected surfaces keep flat tops and steep sides. The sequence runs: a plateau, an extensive flat-topped elevated area bounded by escarpments; a mesa, a large detached flat-topped fragment wider than it is high; a butte, the same body whittled until it is higher than it is wide with only a small flat summit, like the dolerite-capped Three Sisters near Beaufort West; a conical hill or pointed koppie, formed once the cap is breached and the unprotected soft layers weather into a cone; and finally the plain, when the hill is consumed entirely. The basaltic plateau of Lesotho and the high Drakensberg is the igneous version, built of stacked lava flows that behave like horizontal strata.

questions.question: Describe the processes of scarp retreat and back wasting, contrast back wasting with down wasting, and explain how pediments and a pediplain develop.
questions.expected_answer: The cliff at the top of a Karoo slope is attacked by frost wedging its joints and by temperature changes, while thunderstorm runoff guts the soft shale beneath the cap, undermining the cliff so capped blocks break away. The cliff does not become gentler: it keeps roughly the same steep angle but is rebuilt further back, so the whole slope retreats parallel to itself — scarp retreat or parallel retreat, the model Lester King developed on South African landscapes. Erosion that wears slopes back sideways while they keep their shape is back wasting; down wasting, by contrast, lowers a surface from the top, flattening and softening the whole profile. Capped horizontal strata favour back wasting because the resistant cap holds the summit rigid, so the land can only yield at its edges. Each retreating scarp leaves a gently sloping rock floor at its foot called a pediment, and when scarps retreating from opposite sides consume the upland between them, the pediments merge into a wide, nearly level erosion surface — a pediplain — dotted with surviving mesas, buttes and koppies, which describes the Great Karoo.

questions.question: Describe canyon landscapes in horizontal strata with named examples, and show how these landscapes are handled in mapwork: contour signatures, vertical exaggeration and gradient.
questions.expected_answer: A powerful river cutting down through flat-lying strata slices a deep steep-walled canyon whose walls expose the layers in cross-section: hard bands stand as vertical cliffs and soft bands weather back, giving step-like walls. The Fish River Canyon in southern Namibia is the classic African example, with the Blyde River Canyon and Oribi Gorge as South African showpieces; canyons deepen where uplift rejuvenates the river. On a 1:50 000 map, a mesa shows as closed contours with a wide empty summit ringed by tightly crowded contours marking the cliff; a butte is the same signature with a tiny summit; stepped slopes show as alternating bands of crowded and spaced contours; a canyon shows as paired walls of tightly packed contours pinching the river's line. A cross-section is drawn by ticking contour crossings onto a paper strip and transferring them to a height grid. Vertical exaggeration is the vertical scale divided by the horizontal scale: a vertical scale of 1 centimetre to 20 metres is 1:2 000, so against a 1:50 000 horizontal scale the exaggeration is 50 000 divided by 2 000, which is 25 times. Gradient is height difference over horizontal distance in the same units: 200 metres of climb over 1 000 metres is 1 in 5.
